item.title: Geometric Constraints Determine Chemical Bond Parameters: A Unified Scaling Theory of Bond Length, Bond Energy, and Isotope Effects
item.description: Chemical bond parameters—bond length, bond energy, and isotope effects—are traditionally treated as element-specific empirical quantities requiring quantum chemical computation. Here we show that these parameters across the entire periodic table are governed by a single geometric scaling law rooted in coordination polyhedron topology. We introduce geometric looseness (δ), a distributed quantity characterizing deviation from regular polyhedral coordination. A unified bond length formula d = d₀(1+δ) achieves 3.12% equivalent mean error across 82 covalent bonds, outperforming the semiempirical PM7 method (4.62%) at calculator-level cost. A bond energy scaling relation E = k/d reduces covalent bond energy prediction error to 4.2% across 65 bonds and lowers ionic crystal lattice energy error from 4.44% (Born-Landé equation) to 2.73%. The 4.44% Born-Landé deviation falls within the geometric looseness range of non-regular polyhedral coordination (2.6%–6.6%), indicating classical theory's error range is the quantitative manifestation of coordination geometric looseness. A universal isotope correction formula calibrated via diamond-family elements (C/Si/Ge, ε₀=0.045) predicts isotope-induced bond length changes in quantitative agreement with experiment at six orders of magnitude lower cost than path-integral molecular dynamics. A complete 63-element quick-reference table enables instant bond parameter prediction. This framework reframes chemical bonding as a unified geometric scaling theory with immediate utility across chemistry, physics, and materials science.

item.title: Charge from the Triality Grading: Thirds Quantization, Charge Conjugation as Spatial Inversion, and the Glue-Class Structure of Matter on the D4 Vacuum
item.description: In the Selection-Stitch Model the vacuum is a face-centered-cubic lattice, its four-dimensional home is the D4 root lattice, and color is the fixed subalgebra of a twisted triality automorphism sigma acting on so(8). This paper asks where electric charge can live in that structure, and answers with five results, each verified by independent reconstruction of the full construction. First, a no-go: the commutant of the twisted su(3) in so(8) is trivial, so the bond algebra contains no internal hypercharge; any charge is external. Second, an exact normalization: the twisted color roots have squared length 2/3 against the ambient 2, so the color generators carry an index-3 normalization relative to the bond form. Third, the same twist that selects color cyclically permutes the three glue classes of D4*/D4, and the three 8-dimensional matter representations sit one per class: matter is the diamond-type extension of the lattice, and color selection and charge-class rotation are one operator. Fourth, on the full matter sector 8v + 8s + 8c the grading of sigma defines a conserved charge Q = q/3 with q in {0, +1, -1}: charge is quantized in thirds, and every charge sector carries the identical color content 3 + 3bar + 1 + 1. Fifth, spatial inversion conjugates the twist to its inverse and therefore maps Q to -Q: on the grading, charge conjugation is spatial inversion. One simplest identification is also excluded: the structure-fixed coupling ratios 3 and 1/3 fail against renormalization-group running, so any coupling derivation must produce near-equal couplings at the lattice scale. The structure is not prediction-free: because the grading is discrete and exact, millicharged particles are forbidden outright, a standing falsifier against active searches. Two selections remain open and are stated precisely: the mechanism that restricts matter to the charge-triality diagonal the Standard Model occupies, and the integer charge unit that produces +-2/3. Every claim carries a status tag.

item.title: Ion Concentration and Voltage Imaging With Fluorescent Nanodiamonds
item.description: ABSTRACT The nitrogen‐vacancy (NV) center in diamond exists in different charge states with distinct photoluminescence properties, which are sensitive to the nanoscale electrochemical environment. Hence, the NV charge state is emerging as a powerful all‐optical platform for nanoscale sensing and imaging. Although significant progress has been made in engineering near‐surface NV centers in bulk diamond, controlling the NV charge state in fluorescent nanodiamonds (FNDs) has proven challenging, limiting the sensitivity and reliability of FND‐based charge state sensing. Here, we demonstrate reliable, reversible switching between the fluorescent NV 0 and a dark state, likely NV + , in sub‐30 nm FNDs via surface oxidation and hydrogenation, respectively, for single particles and particle powder. In aqueous electrochemical cells, we demonstrate voltage and ion concentration imaging based on the NV charge state in self‐assembled FND layers on transparent substrates. Applied voltages reliably modulate the FND PL with a sensitivity of up to 16 mV Hz −1/2 . FND PL is also modulated by local changes in salt concentration with a sensitivity of up to 1.8% per millimolar NaCl, enabling all‐optical imaging of ion concentration gradients at the microscale. Our results represent a significant step toward realizing fast, stable, and scalable nanoscale charge‐ and voltage‐imaging technologies with sub‐micrometer spatial resolution.

item.title: Electrochemical treatment of dacarbazine and paracetamol in synthetic multi-pharmaceutical hospital wastewater: By-product control and operational window
item.description: Hospital effluents contain mixtures of pharmaceuticals coexisting with complex inorganic and organic backgrounds, posing a challenge to conventional treatment. The electrochemical treatment of a synthetic multi-pharmaceutical hospital effluent containing dacarbazine (DTIC) and paracetamol (PCT) was investigated using boron-doped diamond (BDD) and mixed metal oxide RuO 2 /Ti (MMO) anodes at 10 mA cm -2 . Both pharmaceuticals were effectively removed with the two anodes, although only BDD reduced both compounds below the limit of quantification while DTIC removal with MMO reached 99%, and the two systems operated via contrasting routes: BDD behaved as a non-selective combustion-driven system that delivered higher mineralization while accumulating chlorate and perchlorate, whereas MMO behaved as an active anode that channeled the applied charge preferentially towards the target pharmaceuticals, with lower formation of chlorate and perchlorate. Compound coexistence reduced the degradation rate of both pharmaceuticals, but the effect was anode-dependent: PCT was the most penalized compound with BDD (53% against 24% for DTIC), whereas at MMO the chlorine-mediated pathway deferred DTIC degradation until PCT had been consumed (75% against 62%). Ten transformation intermediates were identified, three of them detected exclusively in the multi-pharmaceutical system and tentatively assigned to homo-dimeric coupling products. In silico ecotoxicity screening predicted these dimeric intermediates as the most concerning species for which predictions could be obtained, across acute aquatic, developmental, and mutagenicity endpoints. An operational window of 0.75-1.0 Ah dm -3 is proposed for MMO, within which pharmaceutical removal increases to over 95% with around 30% lower energy demand than BDD while minimizing chlorate and perchlorate formation.

item.title: Tailoring grain and second-phase particles in 6061 aluminum alloy via cryogenic forging to improve surface quality in single-point diamond turning
item.description: The enhancement of surface quality in ultra-precision machining of aluminum alloys is frequently impeded by coarse grains and second-phase particles. This study investigated microstructural refinement of 6061 aluminum alloy through cryogenic multi-directional forging combined with heat treatment to enhance surface quality in single point diamond turning (SPDT). Samples underwent initial annealing (AT) or solution treatment (ST), followed by 1–9 passes of cryogenic forging, solution treatment, and artificial aging. Microstructural characterization revealed that, compared to AT pretreatment, ST pretreatment suppressed dynamic recovery under cryogenic deformation, yielding higher dislocation density and substructure formation. These provided additional nucleation sites for static recrystallization in subsequent solution treatment, resulting in finer, equiaxed grains. Cryogenic forging fragmented coarse second-phase particles, while solution treatment enhanced their dissolution, reducing particle size and volume fraction. Increased dissolution into the aluminum matrix promoted a more uniform precipitation state, which contributed to improved hardness uniformity. SPDT experiments demonstrated that the refined microstructure reduced grain-boundary steps and defects associated with second-phase particles. Compared with the AT1 sample, the ST9 sample exhibited a decrease in the arithmetic average surface roughness, Ra, from 12.54 nm to 6.81 nm, corresponding to a reduction of 45.7%.

item.title: Nanodiamonds in Filtration and Adsorption Systems: Structure-Property Relationships, Immobilization Strategies, and Emerging Applications
item.description: Nanodiamonds (NDs) combine the exceptional hardness, chemical durability, and thermal stability of bulk diamond with a high surface-to-volume ratio and widely tunable surface chemistry. These properties enable broad control over surface charge, polarity, hydration, and interfacial interactions, making NDs attractive for adsorption and water-treatment applications. Nevertheless, their practical potential in these fields remains substantially underdeveloped relative to the depth of accumulated physicochemical knowledge. This review critically examines known and filtration-relevant interactions between ND surfaces and dissolved species, and evaluates how these interactions could be exploited in adsorption and filtration technologies. We compare the two technologically relevant ND classes-detonation nanodiamonds (DNDs) and high-pressure high-temperature (HPHT) NDs-and analyze the consequences of surface termination, defect structure, nitrogen content, and colloidal state for zeta potential, hydration, and interfacial reactivity in aqueous environments. A particular focus is placed on hydrogenated NDs, which exhibit an unusual combination of strongly positive electrokinetic response, pronounced interfacial water structuring, and surface electronic effects associated with charge transfer and particle structure that distinguish them from oxidized NDs and other carbon nanomaterials. We systematically review documented interactions between ND surfaces and relevant pollutant classes: multivalent metal ions, charged organic molecules, PFAS, and biomolecules, drawing on literature from water treatment, biomedicine, and chromatography to establish the breadth of ND interfacial chemistry. A central argument of this review is that the functional unit in ND-based filtration is the accessible ND surface: immobilization strategies that preserve surface exposure-electrostatic deposition, covalent grafting, and thermally assisted stabilization on inorganic supports-are critically distinguished from embedded composite approaches where ND surfaces are mostly buried and rendered passive. We identify the translation of these immobilization strategies to polymer membrane supports as the principal unresolved engineering challenge, and outline the role of ND structural heterogeneity, long-term surface stability, and scalable deaggregation as key scientific priorities for realizing the full potential of NDs in next-generation filtration systems.

item.title: Investigation of phosphorus-doped nanocrystalline diamond films for effective electron photoemission under picosecond laser pulses
item.description: Phosphorus-doped nanocrystalline diamond (P-NCD) films deposited by the chemical vapor deposition method on conductive silicon substrates have been experimentally studied. The grown 100 nm-thick films were characterized by a high content of the diamond carbon phase, which allowed the films to be doped with phosphorus (during growth) to achieve predominant incorporation of phosphorus atoms into diamond grains rather than at the grain boundaries. The photoemission properties of the grown doped and undoped as-grown NCD films were tested, demonstrating different photoemission properties under the influence of a picosecond laser pulse. For undoped NCD films, the emitted charge increased linearly with increasing laser pulse energy, while for phosphorus-doped P-NCD films, it increased quadratically. It was found that the presence of phosphorus in the doped film was responsible for the change from linear to quadratic. This dependence in photoemission from P-NCD films was observed for the first time. An explanation for the quadratic increase in emitted charge with increasing laser pulse energy is proposed.

item.title: Dynamic Bending Stress Sensing Using NV Centers in a Single-Crystal Diamond MEMS Cantilever
item.description: In this study, a single-crystal diamond (SCD) MEMS cantilever was fabricated using a buried graphite sacrificial-layer process. A region containing nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers formed near the ion-implantation-induced defective layer was directly utilized as the stress-sensing region of the released cantilever, enabling dynamic stress sensing without the use of externally attached nanodiamonds. We investigated the relationship between the stress induced by the cantilever vibration and the peak shift of the fluorescence intensity of the optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectrum. By approximately aligning the static magnetic field with one of the four NV-center crystallographic axes, we were able to evaluate the dependence of the peak shift on stress. Our findings revealed that the peak shift can effectively detect uniaxial stress due to normal vibration. In addition, as the vibration amplitude increased, the magnitude of the ODMR peak shift also increased, showing a trend consistent with previously reported NV-center stress responses. Furthermore, the ODMR shift exhibited periodic modulation corresponding to the cantilever’s vibration phase. These results indicate that NV centers in micromachined SCD cantilevers can be used to detect vibration-induced dynamic bending stress.

item.title: High-quality polycrystalline diamond fabrication from the perspective of zeta-potential-governed seeding
item.description: Abstract Nanodiamond seeding and subsequent polycrystalline diamond growth were investigated on five substrates using two suspensions with opposite zeta-potential signs: a negatively charged H2O-based suspension and a positively charged DMSO-based suspension. Zeta potential, pre-seeding surface roughness, seed density, and film structure were characterized by AFM, SEM, Raman spectroscopy, and XRD. Oppositely charged suspension–substrate pairs generally promoted higher initial seed adsorption. The H2O-based suspension produced the highest seed density on weakly positive Al-free AlN nanorods, whereas the DMSO-based suspension gave higher seed densities on negatively charged substrates such as Si, SiO2, and quartz. However, the final diamond growth behavior was not determined by nominal seed density alone. Substrate morphology, surface roughness, seed aggregation, and seed survival under H2-rich plasma also strongly affected film continuity and crystal quality. These results show that zeta-potential contrast regulates initial nanodiamond adsorption, while the final polycrystalline diamond microstructure is governed by coupled substrate–seed–plasma interactions.

item.title: Boosting high-performance terahertz wave shielding of MXene@BNS/SiCw/SiOC composites by heterogeneous interface engineering and 3D-printed metastructure design
item.description: Abstract The rapid development of terahertz (THz) technology brings about the issue of electromagnetic interference (EMI) pollution. Enormous attention has been attracted to develop high-performance THz EMI shielding materials. Herein, a Ti3C2Tx MXene@BNS/SiCw/SiOC composite with superior THz wave shielding performance is developed through heterogeneous interface engineering. Sucroses are grafted onto BN nanoparticles (BNS) to enhance the interfacial interactions between MXene and BN. Driven by hydrogen bonding, BNS is uniformly dispersed onto the layer surface of Ti3C2Tx. Then, SiC whiskers (SiCw) are also introduced to enhance the heterogeneous interface engineering. The fabrication parameters are optimized through an orthogonal experimental design. The resulting bulk MXene@BNS/SiCw/SiOC composite exhibits a high average SET of 42.3 dB. Its excellent THz wave dissipation capability is attributed to the enhanced interfacial polarization from the numerous heterointerfaces, as well as conductive loss. Subsequently, four types of three-period minimal surface (TPMS) metastructures with Diamond (D), I-Wrapped Parallel (I-WP), Gyroid (G), and Primitive (P) architectures are designed and fabricated via vat photopolymerization 3D printing. Among these, the SET value of the developed D metastructure is improved to 68.3 dB, which is higher than that of most reported EMI shielding materials. Its special porous structure increases the internal multiple reflections of electromagnetic waves, leading to a superior THz wave shielding performance. The architecture also demonstrates hydrophobicity and excellent thermal transfer capability. This work sheds new light on the development of advanced THz wave shielding materials by heterogeneous interface engineering and 3D printed metastructure design.

item.title: Metals, Vol. 16, Pages 948: Effects of Lattice Architecture, Nominal Feature Size and Heat Treatment on the Tensile Behavior of L-PBF-Fabricated Inconel 718 Lattice Structures
item.description: Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF)-fabricated Inconel 718 lattice structures offer considerable potential for lightweight load-bearing applications, but their mechanical integrity depends on architecture, geometric scale, manufacturing defects, and post-processing condition. This study examined the combined effects of Diamond, Gyroid, and Octet architectures, nominal feature sizes of 1.0, 1.25, and 1.5 mm, and four heat-treatment conditions on tensile behavior and fracture characteristics. The specimens were evaluated using explicit-dynamics finite element analysis, room-temperature quasi-static tensile testing, and SEM fractography. A feature-size-dependent reversal in architecture ranking was observed: Gyroid exhibited the highest mean apparent tensile strength among the 1.0 mm lattices across the investigated heat-treatment conditions, whereas Diamond exhibited the highest mean apparent tensile strength among the 1.5 mm lattices across the same conditions. HT-C shifted the tensile response toward higher apparent strength and lower apparent deformation capacity, whereas selected HT-B-treated specimens exhibited more ductile fracture morphologies. These findings show that architecture, nominal feature size, and post-processing condition must be considered jointly when designing L-PBF Inconel 718 lattice components within the investigated design range.

item.title: Reproducibility-Based Field Validation of Complementary Subsurface Sensing Using a Quantum Diamond Magnetometer and Multi-Frequency Ground-Penetrating Radar
item.description: Underground infrastructure inspection requires sensing methods capable of characterizing both ferromagnetic and non-ferromagnetic subsurface features. This study evaluated a portable nitrogen-vacancy (NV) quantum diamond magnetometer (QDM) together with multi-frequency ground-penetrating radar (GPR; 250, 500, and 800 MHz) at a 90 m full-scale pavement test site containing documented subsurface targets. Repeated stationary QDM measurements were first conducted to characterize temporal variability and establish site-specific magnetic baselines, followed by a 1 m interval spatial survey and corresponding GPR measurements. The QDM showed reproducible spatial magnetic patterns despite substantial variability in reinforcement-dense sections, and all 10 cross-session measurements remained within ±1.5 standard deviations of their repeated-measurement baselines. Ferromagnetic targets produced localized magnetic responses, whereas post hoc classification using disturbance-normalized magnetic anomalies showed limited target-level discrimination (AUC = 0.495). GPR likewise showed limited post hoc target classification (500 MHz AUC = 0.472), but section-level radar responses differed significantly across pavement environments. The two modalities exhibited contrasting section-level responses while showing weak and inconsistent point-level correspondence. These results indicate that NV-diamond magnetometry and GPR provide complementary physical information, while repeated magnetic measurements are important for interpreting QDM observations under heterogeneous field conditions.

item.title: Symmetry, Vol. 18, Pages 1448: Theoretical and Numerical Study on Buckling Analysis of Cylindrical Shell Structures by Galerkin and Finite Element Methods
item.description: The structural instability of cylindrical shells has long attracted scholarly attention due to its inherently nonlinear response and extensive engineering relevance. Although numerous investigations have examined buckling phenomena arising from individual loading modes such as axial compression or pure torsion, the complex behavior of shells subjected to simultaneous torsional and axial actions remains comparatively underexplored. In this study, an integrated approach combining theoretical formulations and finite element analyses is employed to comprehensively characterize the buckling responses of cylindrical shells under coupled torsional&ndash;axial loading conditions. The theoretical framework is developed using Donnell&rsquo;s shell theory and solved through the Galerkin approximation. The predicted results exhibit strong agreement with finite element simulations. It is demonstrated that the buckling evolution of cylindrical shells under combined loading markedly differs from that produced by a single load component. Specifically, shells under torsion with minor compression display a stable deformation mode, whereas higher compression induces a transition toward a diamond-shaped buckling pattern. Such findings elucidate the coupled torsion&ndash;compression/tension effects governing buckling instabilities in cylindrical shells, offering valuable insight for the design of load-responsive foldable and origami-inspired structures driven by combined mechanical actions.

item.title: Adoption of Forensic Accounting Techniques and Contemporary Fraud Detection Mechanisms in the Financial Sector in Zimbabwe
item.description: Zimbabwe's financial sector faces a sophisticated wave of financial crime that outpaces traditional compliance-driven, paper-based oversight. This study examines the incorporation of forensic accounting techniques in registered commercial banks and insurance companies in Harare, investigating the gap between formal adoption and practical, real-time day-to-day application. Grounded in Fraud Diamond Theory, Differential Association Theory, and Institutional Theory, the study explains individual drivers of fraud alongside institutional performance dynamics. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was employed. Quantitative questionnaires were gathered from 100 purposively selected oversight professionals and analyzed using SPSS, followed by ten semi-structured thematic interviews analyzed via NVivo. Findings show an industry formally compliant but operationally under-equipped: 92% of institutions remain reliant on compliance checklists, 64% report no predictive analytics, and 72% lack continuous digital surveillance. However, data mining adoption strongly correlates with fraud detection effectiveness (Pearson r = 0.742, p < .01), and machine learning accounts for 61% of financial loss reduction variance. Structural barriers include legacy system incompatibility (68%), prohibitively expensive foreign licensing costs, and an entrenched tick-box culture (82%). A decoupling effect exists where compliance satisfies regulatory mandates on paper while departments remain operationally under-resourced. Compulsory forensic readiness audits and API-integrated systems are recommended.

item.title: Inventory
item.description: The book displayed in the picture probably does not live up to the expectations placed on medieval manuscripts: There are no splendid miniatures, the writing is not really careful. What may be most disconcerting to the reader are the many cancellations and notes that have been hastily written on the mostly empty right columns of the pages. Nevertheless, this book is one of the treasures hosted today in the Main State Archives of Baden-Württemberg in Stuttgart. 1 It is one of the oldest and rarest surviving examples of books produced by the ancient chancery of the Visconti family of Milan. The Visconti ruled the city as princes from the 14 th to the mid-15 th century. When the last male Visconti died, urban unrest broke out as the Milanese wanted to create a republican city-state, the Repubblica Ambrosiana. In the course of these fights, the archives of the Visconti and their treasure were destroyed and almost completely lost. 2 The book itself is a book of treasures as can be read on its cover: It is a liber iocalium , a book of jewels. The two pages displayed above record various rings. Some of them are described with the name of the main gems they were adorned with: The first entry on the left page lists an adamans , which means diamond; the second a zaffirus , a sapphirine, while the next four entries all name the term annulus , which means ring. Two of the entries on this page have been cancelled, and the note on the right column explains that these rings were donated to other people. In fact, these notes make the treasure book even more interesting as we learn not only about the valuable objects and what they looked like, but we also get to know what happened to some of these pieces.
item.dc:creator: Christina Antenhofer

item.title: Modeling Carbon-Based Planets with MAGRATHEA
item.description: A planet's interior structure not only influences its habitability, but it also provides information about the planet's formation and history. In the quest to characterize the variety of planetary discoveries, the most common practice is to rely on our understanding of the Earth's differentiated interior structure, with an iron core and silicate mantle as a starting point. However, recent work by arXiv:2408.07761 [astro-ph.EP] shows that these assumptions may not be true for all planetary systems as the composition of the condensed material can change drastically towards a carbon mantle instead of a silicate one, once the C/O ratio of the system approaches and exceeds approximately 0.9. In an effort to more fully understand the range of possible planetary bodies, we added the ability to model carbon-based mantles to our open-source planetary interior solver, MAGRATHEA. The newly added carbon mantle includes three relevant allotropes of carbon: graphite, diamond, and BC8 (body centered cubic with eight atoms per cell).

item.title: Reducing the domain of discrete multi-time determinantal point processes
item.description: We consider a class of discrete multi-time determinantal point processes whose correlation kernels admit a double-contour integral form, containing Schur processes as simple examples. We show that the form of the correlation kernel is preserved under conditioning of the point process to a restricted domain, however, with an integrand which becomes more complicated and which is characterized by a Riemann-Hilbert problem. We apply our general result to domino tilings of reduced Aztec diamonds and to lozenge tilings of hexagons with holes. Our results show a striking analogy with the Its-Izergin-Korepin-Slavnov method for integrable kernels.

item.title: Adaptive Strategies for GR(1) Games
item.description: We consider two-player GR(1) games on graphs, where the system player Eve must satisfy \[ \Box\Diamond A_1\land\cdots\land\Box\Diamond A_m \;\implies\; \Box\Diamond G_1\land\cdots\land\Box\Diamond G_n \] against the environment player Adam. Here $A_1,\ldots,A_m$ are assumptions on the environment, $G_1,\ldots,G_n$ are guarantees the system must provide, and $\Box\Diamond S$ denotes ``always eventually $S$''. Traditional static strategies are overly conservative: they may actively violate assumptions to trivially satisfy the implication, or abandon all guarantees when any assumption is violated. Existing methods to prevent such behaviors incur doubly exponential blowup. We introduce an adaptive framework treating Adam as a non-adversarial agent with unknown objectives. Eve monitors which assumptions Adam actually meets and adapts her strategy at runtime to maximize satisfied guarantees. Central to our approach is a novel algorithm for monitoring liveness properties $\Box\Diamond S$, enabling Eve to maintain real-time likelihood estimates of which assumptions will be fulfilled. Eve pre-computes strategies optimal for different assumption subsets, deploying a probability distribution over them that dynamically adjusts based on monitor outputs. We prove that when assumptions are violated, Eve's randomized adaptive strategy converges asymptotically to the deterministic strategy maximizing guarantees. A prototype demonstrates effectiveness and superior computational performance compared to the state of the art.

item.title: Beyond sensitivity: mechanism-resolved error budgets for designing quantum sensors
item.description: Quantum sensors are specified by a headline sensitivity, yet applications also demand accuracy and reliability. The dominant limiter of one metric is often known, but no method resolves how interacting mechanisms combine into a signed, per-mechanism budget for each metric. We introduce a framework that computes a sensor's sensitivity, accuracy, and robustness from one open-system simulation and attributes each to its limiting mechanism. For a nitrogen-vacancy diamond ensemble the attribution inverts across metrics: dephasing limits sensitivity, the thermal ground-state shift limits accuracy, and optical leakage limits robustness. At identical sensitivity the recovered-field bias spans $8$ to $1500$\,nT, so tuning to sensitivity alone can miss the accuracy target by two orders of magnitude. The same modeling transfers to a cesium optically pumped magnetometer recording a human magnetocardiogram. As a digital twin, it predicts the gain from addressing each limiter, so sensors can be designed to the required metrics.

item.title: Spatially Resolved Synchrotron X-ray Tomography and Diffraction of Cryogenic Natron and Fluid Inclusions in a Frozen Na-Cl-CO3 Solution
item.description: This dataset contains full-field reconstructed synchrotron X-ray computed microtomography (µCT) and spatially resolved X-ray diffraction (XRD) data of a frozen Na-Cl-CO3 solution. The data reveals the microstructure of the ice, the presence of cryogenic natron Na-Cl-CO3, and the entrapment of primary fluid inclusions within the salt crystals. Sample Preparation: An aqueous solution of 1.0 m NaCl and 0.5 m Na2CO3 was loaded into a 1 mm Kapton capillary. The sample was cooled from 268 K to 205 K at a rate of 6 K/min. Data Collection (K11-DIAD, Diamond Light Source): Tomography (43992.tiff): 1005 projections collected over 180 degrees at 20 keV with a 0.1 s exposure (PCO Edge 5.5). The detector was binned 2x, resulting in a pixel resolution of 2.16 µm. Reconstructed using ASTRA-Toolbox/SAVU. Diffraction (k11-43994_processed.nxs): A 10x10 spatially correlated grid scan using a 25 x 25 µm micro-focused beam (20 keV) collected on a Pilatus 2M (15 s exposure). New data (V2): We have ammended this entry to include the training data, labelled data and output model constructed using the Volume Segmantics Package (https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.04691). The training data consists of tif stacks containing the raw and labelled volumes of 256x256x256 pixels (43902_raw.tif, 43902_labeled.tif,43906_raw.tif, 43906_labeled.tif, 43908_raw.tif,43908_labeled.tif, 43910_raw.tif, 43910_labeled.tif, 43992_raw.tif, 43992_labeled.tif.). This data represents sequential tomographies of the same region in the sample at different temperatures. The yaml file containing the model training characteristics for Volume Segmantics (2d_model_train_settings.yaml) This dataset also includes the final trained UNET pytorch model (2024-10-25_U_NET_PLUS_PLUS__model.pytorch). This model was trained using the VolumeSegmantics package. Details published (https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.04691). New data (V3): All reconstructed tomography data has been added from 269 to 210K (imaging.zip) as 8 bit tiff stacks. All reduced single point diffraction data has been added from 269 to 205K (diffraction_processed.zip). A csv of scan numbers, scan type, and temperature (scans.csv). This data supports the findings in the manuscript Fluid inclusions establish natron as a key astrobiological target on Enceladus".

item.title: llama-annotation-pipeline: Snakemake workflow and documented commands for homology-based and ab initio annotation of the Lama glama genome
item.description: Reproducible Snakemake workflow for the structural annotation of a chromosome-level Lama glama genome assembly by homology transfer and ab initio prediction, with evaluation against an external reference. The workflow generates four proteome sets and a combined candidate reference proteome of 20,708 sequences, stratified into three nested confidence layers: 18,920 high-confidence models with an intact reading frame and detectable homology in an external reference, 1,313 extended-reference models failing one or both criteria, and 475 candidates from the ab initio prediction. The Snakemake workflow covers Liftoff, miniprot, proteome extraction and BUSCO. LiftOn, Helixer, InterProScan and DIAMOND were run manually, with the commands documented in REPRODUCIBILITY.md. No sequence or annotation data are tracked in this repository. The annotation sets and proteomes are deposited separately under CC0-1.0, concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21445839.

item.title: The Composite Polyhedral Boundary Framework: Derivation of Unified Scaling Coefficients across 26 Crystalline Elements
item.description: This work establishes the Hollin-Levine Unified Lattice Framework, a first-principles deterministic model that derives precise scaling coefficients (\Omega) from the interaction between Platonic container geometries and close-packed atomic clusters. By evaluating 26 metallic, covalent, and diamond-structure crystalline elements, the framework demonstrates that macroscopic yield limits are governed by composite boundary-stress correction factors rather than arbitrary curve-fitting heuristics. The manuscript provides complete operator domain and codomain specifications, an explicit 26-element residual appendix demonstrating an overall RMSD of 12.4 MPa and a MAPE of 4.2%, and rigorous baseline literature citations.

item.title: Hamiltonian Statics under sp3 Hybridization Tetrahedral Constraints and Maximal Packing Coset Classification of Diamond Cubic Systems
item.description: This paper extends the framework of Hamiltonian field theory and hierarchical coset classification, established in previous works, from non-equilibrium dissipative growth dynamics to the limit of static stability under equilibrium thermodynamic boundary conditions. The rigid three-dimensional geometric constraints of the tetrahedral coordination (bond angle 109.5^\circ) originating from the sp3 hybridized orbitals of carbon atoms are formulated as a higher-order gauge-invariant Hamiltonian. By introducing the fluid dynamical chaotic operators defined in previous frameworks, this study specifies the deterministic mechanism wherein external fluid turbulence is algebraically attenuated near the energetic local maxima of the covalent bonding barriers. Investigating the variational minima of the total free energy functional demonstrates that the infinite-dimensional configuration space of maximum density packing is projected and degenerated into exactly two static cosets that preserve the invariant symmetries of the crystallographic space group Fd\bar{3}m.

item.title: Discrete Spacetime Topological Network,DSTN.(Basic Theory And Core Derivations )/阴阳爻网络模型DSTN(基础理论与核心推导)
item.description: This study presents the "DSTN(Discrete Spacetime Topological Network)", an interdisciplinary research program that integrates Eastern wisdom with modern mathematical and physical sciences. It aims to resolve the unification problem of quantum mechanics and general relativity, and reconstruct the cognitive framework of the cosmic origin. Breaking through the traditional reductionist paradigm, the model draws inspiration from the holistic and generative perspectives in I Ching and Daoist thought, establishing five core axioms: 1. The ultimate fundamental unit is the "Yao" (±1), representing the binary states of Yin and Yang;2. The universe is a discrete dynamic network formed by the connections of Yao;3. Spacetime, matter, and interactions are all emergent phenomena of network evolution;4. The network follows the conservation of topological charge;5. The network evolves toward the minimization of energy. Based on the axiomatic system, the model naturally derives three core laws: the law of combinatorial creation, the law of closed-loop stability, and the law of threshold realization. It also proposes key geometric conjectures: the network spontaneously organizes into a dual triangular pyramid as the basic unit and a nested diamond lattice topology, giving rise to characteristic numbers such as 9, 27, 36, and 108 (where 108 = 2²×3³, the critical threshold for matter transitioning from "virtual state" to "real state"). These numbers not only correlate with key parameters in particle physics and cosmology but also align with core symbols in Eastern culture. The model constructs a complete mathematical framework and dynamic evolution path. Based on the evolutionary laws of the discrete network, it presents a derivation pathway toward the core equations of general relativity and quantum mechanics, offering a feasible approach to achieving compatibility between the continuous limit and existing theories. It also clarifies the emergent mechanism of fundamental physical constants (e.g., the speed of light c, Planck constant h, fine-structure constant α), and presents a quantitative association framework linking them to network parameters. As a testable scientific program, the model provides twelve specific physical predictions: including the cubic power distribution of dark matter mass spectrum, the large-scale attenuation and 108-fold resonance peak of cosmic microwave background radiation, the scarcity of high-redshift galaxies, and the weak dispersion effect of gravitational waves. These predictions clearly distinguish themselves from mainstream paradigms and can be verified by next-generation detectors and observation equipment. This research offers a new exploration path for quantum gravity and unified field theory. We invite scholars in mathematics, physics, computer science, and other fields to jointly advance axiom formalization, numerical simulation, and experimental verification, and decode the deep geometric and numerical order of the universe. Author Note: The author is an independent researcher, and the "Researcher" label in this record refers to a general academic identity, not a formal professional title. This section presents the foundational theoretical core of the Yin-Yang Network Cosmic Model. For extended applications of this theory and related scientific papers, please refer to the following DOIs: DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18426000.DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18493628

item.title: Reproducibility archive: noise and selection bias in the Sverdlov–Bombelli nested-interval sum (flat-spacetime sprinkling test)
item.description: This archive contains the complete code, analysis scripts and raw simulation output for the first sprinkling test of the Sverdlov–Bombelli nested-interval construction for recovering curvature from a causal set. The Sverdlov–Bombelli construction (Class. Quantum Grav. 26, 075011, 2009) recovers the Ricci scalar and the timelike Ricci component from interval volumes measured at a family of nested scales. It has been cited since 2009 but, to our knowledge, had never been confronted with an actual Poisson sprinkling. The accompanying paper tests its auxiliary nested sum in flat four-dimensional Minkowski space, where the sum has expectation zero identically, so that the estimator's bias and noise are isolated from any curvature signal. Three results are established, and everything needed to reproduce them is here. The cutoff on sub-interval cardinality is biased, exactly and calculably. Because cardinality is the same quantity whose fluctuation the estimator averages, thresholding on it selects on the noise. The resulting bias has an exact parameter-free form — a Poisson point mass one count below the threshold, integrated over the diamond — which reproduces all 35 measured cell means without being fitted to them. The variance obeys an exact deterministic integral law, Var(S) = M + n̄G, derived from the Mecke equation. Parameter-free quadrature confirms the dominant pair coefficient G at about the percent level at every cutoff. G spans a factor of 700 across the sampled cutoff range, so the cutoff is not a free regulator whose value may be chosen for convenience. The bias is removable without leaving the causal set. Splitting the sprinkling by independent Bernoulli marks, selecting sub-intervals on one copy and estimating from the other, gives an embedding-free estimator that is exactly unbiased in the mean. Its variance is bounded below by the same deterministic functionals evaluated at the mean selection weight, and the measurement reproduces that bound at the percent level. Contents code/ — the two sprinkling pipelines (literal, oracle and thinned cutoffs), the deterministic quadrature for the variance functionals, the bootstrap analyses, the figure generator, and the archive/verification tooling. shards/ — raw per-replicate output, one compressed array per ensemble. records/ — analysis logs, including the recorded post-mortem of a superseded variance reference. README.md — per-script documentation, the exact commands used, the ensembles and seeds behind every published number, and the expected values a re-run should reproduce. Notes on reproducibility Every published number is tied to an explicit list of input files rather than to a directory listing: the analysis scripts require a manifest for any run that generates publication output, and record SHA-256 checksums of the files they read. The scripts also refuse to pool distinct ensembles. Diagnostic and production runs are separate ensembles, and combining them silently yields replicate-weighted averages that look like valid results; this occurred during development and produced an apparent inconsistency that took a dedicated investigation to resolve. The guard is enforced in code, not left to discipline, and the README documents which script enforces which check. One superseded quantity is preserved deliberately. An intermediate variance reference was wrong twice before it was right, and the historical function and its output are retained alongside the corrected version so that the recorded post-mortem reproduces exactly. It is clearly marked and must not be used for new comparisons. Requires Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib. CuPy is optional and used only for GPU acceleration of the sprinklers, which fall back to NumPy.

item.title: PAC–μ⁸ Foundations and Audit Trilogy: Physical Objecthood, Dynamical Complex Structure, and Cross-Platform Time-Crystal Certification Description
item.description: This Zenodo collection brings together three coordinated studies from the PAC–(\mu^8) research programme. The papers address three distinct but connected questions: [\text{What qualifies as a physical object?}] [\text{Under what dynamical conditions does a complex structure emerge on a real state space?}] [\text{Can an experimental certification framework transfer across physically different realizations of time-crystalline order?}] The collection is organized as a progression from philosophical reconstruction, through mathematical audit, to public-data and cross-platform empirical assessment. 1. PAC–OBJ–001 From Position to Certified Object: A Historical and Modal Reconstruction of Physical Objecthood This paper reconstructs the development of physical objecthood from geometrical position and the Newtonian material point to relativistic events and worldlines, field modes, spectral packets, experimental records, and certified object classes. Its central proposal is that physical objecthood should not be treated as a primitive visual or spatial fact. Instead, an object may be understood as a process-generated structure that remains identifiable through persistence, invariant relations, recordability, separability from background, and robustness under admissible perturbations and changes of protocol. The paper introduces the PAC distinction between: [\text{field existence},\qquad\text{mode existence},\qquad\text{certified object status}.] It does not claim that observation creates physical reality, nor that all objects are periodic resonances. Its narrower thesis is that public and scientifically warranted object reference depends on stable relations among dynamics, boundaries, records, reconstruction, and certification. 2. PAC–MAT–001 Complex Structure from Real Reversible Dynamics: A Domain, Kernel, Uniqueness, Irreducibility, Spectral-Support, and Positive-Energy Audit This paper provides a mathematical audit of the claim that an orthogonal complex structure can arise from real reversible dynamics. For a strongly continuous orthogonal one-parameter group on a real Hilbert space, the skew-adjoint generator (A) admits a polar decomposition on the closed dynamical support (\ker A)^\perp \overline{\operatorname{Ran}|A|},] of the form [A=J_A|A|,] where [J_A^*=-J_A,\qquadJ_A^2=-I,\qquad[J_A,|A|]=0.] The audit shows that: mere invertibility is insufficient; norm-preserving orthogonal dynamics are required; the complex structure is canonically selected only on the non-stationary dynamical support; the kernel of (A) does not acquire a preferred complex structure without additional choices; positive energy is not required for the mathematical existence of (J_A); a positive-energy and future-time convention selects the Schrödinger orientation and the positive Hamiltonian[H=\hbar|A|;] the positive operator[K=|A|^2]does not by itself determine phase orientation; irreducibility and a spectral gap are not required for existence, although they can matter for uniqueness under larger symmetry algebras and for perturbative stability. The paper therefore narrows the legitimate claim: the imaginary unit may represent the quarter-turn structure canonically associated with oriented real orthogonal dynamics on their dynamical support. It does not claim that this construction alone derives the Born rule, quantum measurement, relativistic quantum field theory, particle content, gauge groups, or the Standard Model. 3. PAC–DTC–002–R1M Cross-Platform Transfer Audit of Multi-Witness Certification in a Room-Temperature Prethermal Time Crystal This study examines whether the multi-witness certification architecture developed for a many-body-localized discrete time crystal on a superconducting quantum processor can be transferred literally to a physically different realization: a room-temperature prethermal discrete time crystal in a three-dimensional dipolar (^{13}\mathrm C) nuclear-spin ensemble in diamond. The literal transfer fails at the level of witness availability and physical mechanism. The original MBL-DTC protocol relies on observables such as processor echo, localization, programmable initial-state testing, and finite-size spin-glass order. These measurements do not transfer directly to a prethermal NMR ensemble governed by different stabilization and failure mechanisms. Under the frozen literal witness set, the direct evidence coverage is only [\kappa_{\mathrm{direct}}^{\mathrm{literal}}=25%,] or [\kappa_{\mathrm{augmented}}^{\mathrm{literal}}=37.5%] when partial literature-level evidence is included. The appropriate formal output is therefore [\mathsf{INDETERMINATE},] rather than PASS or FAIL. The study then identifies a more general transfer principle: [\boxed{\text{cross-platform certification should preserve evidence roles and failure logic,}\newline\text{not necessarily identical experimental observables.}}] For the prethermal time-crystal platform, relevant evidence roles include subharmonic locking, persistence, perturbation rigidity, interaction dependence, mechanism controls, separation from alternative phases, initial-state robustness, and collective order. Because this evidence-role map was constructed after inspection of the target experiment, the result is classified as a retrospective interface reconstruction rather than a prospective cross-platform validation. The current evidence level is therefore reported as [\mathrm{E2!-!META},] not E4. Unified Contribution Taken together, the three studies establish a disciplined sequence: [\boxed{\begin{aligned}\text{process and record}&\longrightarrow\text{qualified physical objecthood},\\text{real reversible dynamics}&\longrightarrow\text{complex phase structure on dynamical support},\\text{platform-specific observables}&\longrightarrow\text{common evidence roles and controlled certification}.\end{aligned}}] The collection develops PAC–(\mu^8) primarily as a framework for philosophical clarification, mathematical interface analysis, and auditable public-data research. It emphasizes explicit assumptions, domain restrictions, carrier separation, evidence coverage, negative results, and the formal possibility of an INDETERMINATE outcome. The collection does not claim that: PAC–(\mu^8) has been experimentally verified as a whole; the three papers constitute a completed unified physical theory; complex structure alone derives all of quantum mechanics; time-crystal experiments validate a universal value of (\mu_*); many-body localization and prethermalization are the same physical mechanism; all physical objects are resonances; public-data reconstruction is equivalent to performing a new experiment. No new physical experiment was conducted in these studies. The empirical component consists of independent secondary analysis and methodological comparison based on published experimental results and publicly described data products. The collection is intended to demonstrate a more modest but testable research standard: [\boxed{\text{a PAC claim should be accepted only after its assumptions, carrier, records,}\newline\text{evidence role, uncertainty, and failure conditions have been made explicit.}}] Suggested Keywords PAC–(\mu^8); physical objecthood; certified object; process ontology; complex structure; real Hilbert space; skew-adjoint generator; polar decomposition; imaginary unit; reversible dynamics; positive energy; discrete time crystal; prethermal time crystal; many-body localization; cross-platform certification; public-data research; evidence-role mapping; mathematical audit; philosophy of physics

item.title: Reproducibility archive: Ricci-curvature recovery in the Sverdlov–Bombelli nested-interval construction (four-geometry causal-set sprinkling study)
item.description: This archive contains the manuscript, supplementary material, complete analysis code, sampler versions, and raw per-replicate simulation output for a preregistered four-geometry test of the Sverdlov–Bombelli nested-interval construction for recovering Ricci curvature from a causal set. The Sverdlov–Bombelli construction (Class. Quantum Grav. 26, 075011, 2009) recovers the Ricci scalar R and the timelike Ricci component R00 from interval volumes measured at a family of nested scales. A companion paper (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22137975) established the bias and noise properties of its auxiliary nested sum in flat spacetime. This work is the curved-space test: whether the construction separates the two curvature components in geometries where they are actually present. Four geometries are sprinkled — radiation and dust FLRW, de Sitter and anti-de Sitter — with acceptance bands frozen in advance. Structure. Maximally symmetric backgrounds satisfy R00 = -R/4 and therefore explore only one direction in curvature-parameter space; the de Sitter and anti-de Sitter arms measure only that combination, which is detected against zero at 61σ and 64σ and reverses sign correctly. Independent validation of the two component responses falls to the FLRW arms. The 2x2 inversion is algebraically invertible but strongly ill-conditioned throughout the tested range: the design rows are 4.4 degrees apart in the production dust arm, closing to 2.0 degrees as the cutoff rises, with corr(R,R00) = +0.997. Registered outcome. All six registered marginal and sign-gate criteria pass, and a dedicated unbanded R arm returns R T^2 = 0.13235 +/- 0.02734 against truth 0.13038. The preregistered global closure nonetheless fails, with lambda_00 lying 3.39σ from unity against a registered 3σ limit. Diagnosis. The miss is a finite-size model discrepancy: the registered design is first order in curvature while the observable is the unexpanded finite-diamond continuum volume, a 4.4% difference invisible in marginal bands but decisive along the covariance's stiff direction. An oracle intervention using converged continuum volumes returns lambda_R = 1.0000 +/- 0.0238 and lambda_00 = 1.0020 +/- 0.0091. A first-order sampler defect found and corrected during the programme is also documented here, with both the historical and corrected sampler versions retained. Contents manuscript/ — the paper and supplementary material (LaTeX source and PDF), the four figures, and the Figure 4 eigenvector loadings. scripts/ — the frozen preregistration, both design modules, the arm-scoring and global-fit analyses, the dedicated-R ratio analysis, the oracle truncation-corrected fit, the proper-time sensitivity study, the figure generator, and the manifest tooling. scripts2/ — the sampler chain (historical and corrected), the sampler unit suite, and the inverse-CDF convergence suite with its machine-readable results. shards/ — raw per-replicate output: the four registered arms, the flat-gate ensemble, and the 7.7 million replicate dedicated-R arm. MANIFEST.json — SHA-256 hash, size, role and provenance for every artifact, plus the command reproducing each table and figure. Notes on reproducibility Every artifact is hashed in MANIFEST.json, and verify_manifest.py re-checks every hash and exits nonzero on any mismatch. Each shard additionally carries its own recorded provenance — geometry, curvature parameter, seed, replicate count, density and code version — read from the file itself rather than inferred from its filename. The dedicated-R shard is identified by that recorded content and hash-checked against the file the published Section 4.2 numbers were computed from, so a renamed or substituted shard cannot silently enter the archive; this guard caught exactly that error during assembly. Both the defective and corrected sampler versions are retained, with distinct code-version strings, and the analysis refuses to pool shards across them. The convergence suite regenerates the sampler-defect evidence from a fresh seed and enforces, rather than assumes, that the two sampler versions consume identical random streams. Requires Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib. CuPy is optional and used only for GPU acceleration of the sprinklers, which fall back to NumPy.

item.title: Material Field Structure
item.description: Conventional material science describes what materials do in exquisite empirical detail, but it has no single mechanism that explains why any of it is true. This paper presents the UST (Unified Substrate Theory) framework for materials, in which the substrate, a continuous tension field underlying all matter and energy, is the actual actor. Materials are not independent objects sitting in space. They are regions where the substrate locked itself into stable geometric configurations: frozen or semi-frozen field patterns that we then measure and call iron, glass, diamond, or silicon. Every material property, stiffness, conductivity, ductility, melting point, optical behavior, fracture toughness, is a direct consequence of that geometry. When a material deforms under load, its geometry is shifting. When it fails, the geometry collapsed past its stability threshold. When we engineer a material, we are choosing and stabilizing a geometry. (The Universal Baseline Level) UBL provides the organizing principle: the substrate always seeks the lowest-tension, lowest-noise configuration available. UBL = 1 is the fully quiet state, perfect balance. All material behavior can be read as the substrate's continuous effort to find or maintain that balance, and all material engineering can be reframed as geometry design. This paper builds that framework section by section, covering field geometry types, tension modes, curvature, shear structures, oscillation behavior, boundaries, defects, material classes, and a design philosophy for working with the field instead of against it. This work is part of a larger collection of UST documents. The other versions available in the DOI record are not revisions of this document. They are separate papers written for different purposes. Some versions present the full mathematical proofs behind the update rules, others provide a technical physical description of substrate behavior, and others are formal proof papers built around the Universal Balance Laws. Together, these documents form a complete set: a plain‑language booklet, a physical description paper, and full mathematical proof papers, each offering a different perspective on the same underlying theory. If you have questions or want to discuss the work, you can contact me directly at dustin@unifiedsubstratetheory.com Don't be shy. I want to discuss science. It is fun and should be. Reachout and lets get started on new discoveries.

item.title: Spatially Resolved Synchrotron X-ray Tomography and Diffraction of Cryogenic Natron and Fluid Inclusions in a Frozen Na-Cl-CO3 Solution
item.description: This dataset contains full-field reconstructed synchrotron X-ray computed microtomography (µCT) and spatially resolved X-ray diffraction (XRD) data of a frozen Na-Cl-CO3 solution. The data reveals the microstructure of the ice, the presence of cryogenic natron Na-Cl-CO3, and the entrapment of primary fluid inclusions within the salt crystals. Sample Preparation: An aqueous solution of 1.0 m NaCl and 0.5 m Na2CO3 was loaded into a 1 mm Kapton capillary. The sample was cooled from 268 K to 205 K at a rate of 6 K/min. Data Collection (K11-DIAD, Diamond Light Source): Tomography (43992.tiff): 1005 projections collected over 180 degrees at 20 keV with a 0.1 s exposure (PCO Edge 5.5). The detector was binned 2x, resulting in a pixel resolution of 2.16 µm. Reconstructed using ASTRA-Toolbox/SAVU. Diffraction (k11-43994_processed.nxs): A 10x10 spatially correlated grid scan using a 25 x 25 µm micro-focused beam (20 keV) collected on a Pilatus 2M (15 s exposure). New data (V2): We have ammended this entry to include the training data, labelled data and output model constructed using the Volume Segmantics Package (https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.04691). The training data consists of tif stacks containing the raw and labelled volumes of 256x256x256 pixels (43902_raw.tif, 43902_labeled.tif,43906_raw.tif, 43906_labeled.tif, 43908_raw.tif,43908_labeled.tif, 43910_raw.tif, 43910_labeled.tif, 43992_raw.tif, 43992_labeled.tif.). This data represents sequential tomographies of the same region in the sample at different temperatures. The yaml file containing the model training characteristics for Volume Segmantics (2d_model_train_settings.yaml) This dataset also includes the final trained UNET pytorch model (2024-10-25_U_NET_PLUS_PLUS__model.pytorch). This model was trained using the VolumeSegmantics package. Details published (https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.04691). New data (V3): All reconstructed tomography data has been added from 269 to 210K (imaging.zip) as 8 bit tiff stacks. All reduced single point diffraction data has been added from 269 to 205K (diffraction_processed.zip). A csv of scan numbers, scan type, and temperature (scans.csv). This data supports the findings in the manuscript Fluid inclusions establish natron as a key astrobiological target on Enceladus".

item.title: DORA Commitment – L'Europe unie / United Europe (2026)
item.description: This Zenodo record documents the formal commitment of L’Europe unie / United Europe (Paris, France; Print ISSN 2780-8173; Online ISSN and ISSN-L 2743-4052) to the principles of the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA). The public statement was adopted on 28 August 2026. On the same date, the journal submitted its organisational signature to DORA and received formal confirmation that the submission had entered staff review. Approval and publication in the official DORA signatory database remain pending. Founded in Paris in 2007, L’Europe unie / United Europe already implements the core principles of responsible research assessment through merit-based editorial evaluation, independent double-blind peer review by at least two external academic experts, systematic anti-plagiarism verification, transparent authorship requirements, responsible presentation of citation indicators, article-level DOI identification, Diamond Open Access and publicly available editorial, correction and retraction policies. The journal evaluates articles according to their originality, methodological rigour, quality of sources, ethical compliance, relevance and contribution to knowledge. Journal-level metrics are not used as substitutes for assessing the scholarly quality of individual articles, authors or researchers. The journal’s commitment to international editorial quality is further demonstrated by continuous publication since 2007, an international scientific board, a rejection rate exceeding 50%, international authorship and inclusion in ERIH PLUS, DOAJ, EBSCO Political Science Complete, CEEOL, ProQuest, HeinOnline and other recognised academic discovery and bibliographic services. Journal-level metrics are not used as substitutes for assessing the scholarly quality of individual articles, authors or researchers. item.title: Nested Return in a Composite Diamond Clock: A Welded-Seam Audit of Phase Projection, Thermal Nulling, and Residual-Burden Migration
item.description: Solid-state frequency references based on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond offer compactness, robustness, and high emitter density, but their electronic zero-field splitting DD exhibits substantial temperature sensitivity near room temperature. This study performs an independent structural analysis of the composite diamond-clock experiment reported by Lourette et al. (Physical Review Applied 25, 064046, 2026). The analysis identifies two experimentally distinct operations acting on different representational spaces. First, the two-tone zero-field-splitting protocol with eight-phase cycling (TTZFS-8) acts on phase-resolved observations to suppress pulse-error-generated spectral components and restore the desired half-sum transition mode. Second, a composite D/QD/Q estimator acts on the resulting two-channel detuning vector to preserve the common local-oscillator correction while nulling first-order thermal drift. In normalized form, the thermal operation satisfies the exact first-order conditions wTT1=1,wTTλ=0,\mathbf w_T^{\mathsf T}\mathbf 1=1, \qquad \mathbf w_T^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\lambda}=0, exposing the estimator as a simultaneous preservation-and-annihilation functional. The unequal fractional thermal coefficients of DD and QQ further establish first-order identifiability of oscillator and temperature contributions. These operations compose into a typed nested architecture, (SD,SQ)→Rϕ,D⊕Rϕ,Q(d,q)→RTuψ.(\mathbf S_D,\mathbf S_Q) \xrightarrow{\mathcal R_{\phi,D}\oplus\mathcal R_{\phi,Q}} (d,q) \xrightarrow{\mathcal R_T} u_\psi . The published ten-day experiment provides the empirical witness: the composite reference becomes more stable than either individual channel beyond approximately 200200 s, with source-reported improvements of roughly 4×4\times at 200200 s and 200×200\times at 2×1052\times10^5 s relative to the DD-only reference. The source systematic budget reveals a further structural consequence. Once the dominant thermal contribution is suppressed, the ordering of the remaining error budget changes and radio-frequency power sensitivity becomes the leading estimated nonthermal residual among the tabulated composite contributions. This transition is formalized here as residual-burden migration: successful local closure can change the identity of the governing residual rather than abolishing burden altogether. Within Structura Reditus / Generative Collapse Dynamics, the resulting operators are interpreted as Tier-2 domain closures only. The analysis does not infer canonical τR\tau_R or welded continuity because the published experiment does not supply the frozen temporal return contract, seam-accounting profile, return credit, residual tolerance, or RunID required for a Tier-0 UMCP weld verdict. The native physical mapping is therefore supported while canonical weld status remains non-evaluable.

item.title: Dynamic Bending Stress Sensing Using NV Centers in a Single-Crystal Diamond MEMS Cantilever
item.description: In this study, a single-crystal diamond (SCD) MEMS cantilever was fabricated using a buried graphite sacrificial-layer process. A region containing nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers formed near the ion-implantation-induced defective layer was directly utilized as the stress-sensing region of the released cantilever, enabling dynamic stress sensing without the use of externally attached nanodiamonds. We investigated the relationship between the stress induced by the cantilever vibration and the peak shift of the fluorescence intensity of the optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectrum. By approximately aligning the static magnetic field with one of the four NV-center crystallographic axes, we were able to evaluate the dependence of the peak shift on stress. Our findings revealed that the peak shift can effectively detect uniaxial stress due to normal vibration. In addition, as the vibration amplitude increased, the magnitude of the ODMR peak shift also increased, showing a trend consistent with previously reported NV-center stress responses. Furthermore, the ODMR shift exhibited periodic modulation corresponding to the cantilever’s vibration phase. These results indicate that NV centers in micromachined SCD cantilevers can be used to detect vibration-induced dynamic bending stress.

item.title: Extrusion-based additive manufacturing of zinc bone scaffolds based on triply periodic minimal surfaces
item.description: Extrusion-based additive manufacturing is an emerging approach for fabricating architecturally complex biodegradable metallic bone implants, enabling zinc (Zn) to be processed into intricate scaffold architectures. Here, triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) Zn scaffolds with gyroid, diamond, and I-WP architectures were fabricated by extrusion-based additive manufacturing followed by debinding and sintering. Scaffolds with solid fractions of 20, 30, and 40 vol% were produced, and the 30 vol% scaffolds were selected for characterization. All architectures retained TPMS geometries and exhibited interconnected pore networks with open porosities exceeding 55%, while the gyroid showed the highest shape fidelity. Degradation rates decreased from 0.070–0.087 mm/year at day 7 to 0.039–0.052 mm/year at day 28, with the diamond degrading slowest. Before immersion, the diamond exhibited the highest compressive strength (5.5 ± 0.4 MPa) and elastic modulus (0.67 ± 0.19 GPa). During immersion, compressive strength increased due to corrosion-product deposition. Finite element and computational fluid dynamics analyses revealed architecture-dependent mechanical and transport behavior, with the gyroid showing the highest permeability and lowest pressure drop. All scaffolds supported preosteoblast attachment, with the gyroid showing the highest metabolic activity. These findings demonstrate that TPMS architecture strongly governs the structural, degradation, mechanical, transport, and biological performance of extrusion-printed Zn scaffolds.

item.title: Multiscale finite element modeling of macro-encapsulated phase-change material in 3D-Printed concrete walls under Riyadh climatic conditions
item.description: Phase-change materials (PCMs) are widely used in building systems to control indoor temperature fluctuations and improve energy efficiency. This study conducts a multiscale finite element investigation of the thermal performance of three-dimensional (3D) printed concrete walls incorporating hollow ceramsite (HC) macro-encapsulated PCM under the climatic conditions of Riyadh. A two-scale modeling approach wherein a concrete/HC-PCM unit cell is used to estimate the effective thermal conductivity of the thermal storage concrete is developed. The predicted values are validated against experimental data from the literature, followed by implementation in dynamic wall-scale simulations. The effects of the HC-PCM volume fraction, PCM melting–solidification temperature, wall infill geometry, and multiple PCM melting ranges on thermal regulation are evaluated. The results indicated that increasing the HC-PCM volume fraction improved thermal regulation; a 0.3 HC-PCM volume fraction reduced the peak inner-wall temperature by ∼1.2 °C compared with the wall without PCM. The PCM transition temperature strongly affected seasonal performance; a 30–32 °C range was the most suitable for summer, whereas lower ranges of 15–17 °C and 18–20 °C were more effective in winter. Among the investigated wall geometries, the diamond infill produced the lowest mean temperature and decrement factor, demonstrating the best thermal damping performance. In addition, using two PCMs with different melting ranges reduced the inner-wall temperature swing by ∼45% compared to that of a single-PCM system. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing PCM properties and printed wall geometry for passive thermal regulation in hot arid climates.

item.title: Treatment of mining wastewater polluted with cyanide by electrooxidation: A mechanistic study, with integrated Modeling and kinetic study
item.description: Electrooxidation offers a promising approach for treating cyanide-contaminated mining wastewater, but performance depends on both electrode material and operating conditions. This study integrates a mechanistic investigation with regression modeling and kinetic analysis to evaluate cyanide removal using boron-doped diamond (BDD), mixed metal oxide (MMO), and graphite anodes. A 3 2 full factorial design was applied, varying current density (10–1000 A m −2 ) and anode type, with additional tests in real mining waters to assess matrix effects. Time-resolved measurements allowed kinetic modeling in MATLAB, targeting reduction of cyanide to below 1 mg dm −3 . Mechanistic pathways were elucidated through ion chromatography and supported by literature, revealing that BDD facilitates both direct oxidation and sulfate-mediated radical generation, while MMO and graphite operate primarily via chlorine-mediated indirect oxidation. BDD consistently achieved the fastest and most complete cyanide removal, with higher current densities driving progression toward highly oxidized chlorine species. MMO demonstrated moderate efficiency, limited by its lower oxygen evolution overpotential, and graphite showed poor performance due to surface degradation at higher current densities and low anodic potential. Regression modeling identified log-transformed current density and water source as significant predictors of early-stage cyanide removal, while electrode material controlled final removal performance. The combined mechanistic and statistical insights support empirical process interpretation within the investigated operating range and provide guidance for further optimization of electrochemical cyanide remediation while considering byproduct formation.

item.title: Transfer of Freestanding Fluoropolymer Films for Advanced Semiconductor Devices
item.description: High-quality dielectric films are essential for fabricating advanced electronic devices, but their direct deposition often degrades the films and their underlying interfaces, which compromises device performance, especially on sensitive or low-adhesion surfaces. To overcome these limitations, film transfer methods enable the integration of high-quality dielectric films onto such surfaces without damaging the underlying interfaces. However, existing transfer methods have predominantly focused on high-dielectric-constant (high-κ) materials, leaving a critical gap for transferable, high-quality low-κ alternatives, which are required for enabling low-power and high-speed electronics. Herein, we address this need by demonstrating a method to integrate freestanding low-κ fluoropolymer dielectric films with smooth surface morphology onto diverse substrates, including low-adhesion surfaces like hydrogen-terminated diamond. The transferred films revealed high breakdown fields of 8.0 ± 1.2 MV cm-1, with leakage current density remaining typically below 10-7 A cm-2 before the breakdown. The incorporation of these fluoropolymer films as gate dielectrics in p-channel hydrogen-terminated diamond field-effect transistors resulted in transfer and output characteristics with negligible hysteresis, high channel mobility (≈400 cm2 V-1 s-1), and a low interface trap density (≤3 × 1011 cm-2 eV-1). These findings highlight the versatility of the transfer method and position freestanding fluoropolymers as a promising platform for forming high-quality dielectric/semiconductor interfaces for advanced electronics.

item.title: Direct observation of shock-induced formation of davemaoite, Ca-perovskite
item.description: Perovskite-structured silicates are key minerals of Earth’s lower mantle and have also been identified in shocked meteorites as the (Mg,Fe)SiO3-perovskite phase, bridgmanite. In contrast, CaSiO3-perovskite (davemaoite) has never been found in meteorites and is known only from rare inclusions in deep-mantle diamonds. This contrast highlights a fundamental gap: while natural samples provide indirect evidence for silicate perovskites under shock conditions, laboratory dynamic compression experiments have yet to directly capture perovskite transitions in either MgSiO3 or CaSiO3, likely due to kinetic limitations imposed by nanosecond timescales. Here we present the in situ, atomic-scale observations of CaSiO3-perovskite formation under dynamic compression. Using nanosecond laser-driven shocks and ultrafast X-ray diffraction (XRD) at SACLA, we tracked the transformation of CaSiO3 from low-pressure phases to an amorphous state, and ultimately to davemaoite above ~91(10) GPa, suggesting a disorder–order transformation pathway toward reconstructive crystallization on nanosecond timescales. Upon release, davemaoite undergoes amorphization via a transient low-symmetry phase. These observations provide direct structural evidence for silicate perovskite formation under dynamic loading, resolving a long-standing experimental problem and establishing dynamic compression as an effective route to probe deep-mantle minerals relevant to Earth and Ca-rich exoplanet interiors. Shock compression is an effective approach for studying materials under extreme conditions. Using X-ray diffraction, Lee et al. observe shock-induced davemaoite formation, demonstrating that silicate perovskite can crystallize on nanosecond timescales.

item.title: Confined shear-induced structure discretization enables re-entrant super-repellent metals
item.description: Re-entrant structures are fundamental to achieving robust liquid repellency, especially for low-surface-tension liquids. However, existing fabrication techniques often face a trade-off among mechanical durability, substrate geometry compatibility, large-area processing, and rapid production. Metals, with their inherent robustness, offer a promising substrate, but direct and efficient machining of metallic re-entrant structures remains a significant challenge. Here, we present a one-step mechanical cutting strategy, termed confined shear-induced structure discretization (CSSD), to directly fabricate high-density re-entrant architectures on planar and curved metallic surfaces. By designing a cave-trapezoid composite tool, we achieve a controlled transition from continuous ridges to discrete re-entrant units during ultra-precision diamond turning. The resulting metallic surfaces sustain a super-repellent Cassie–Baxter state for a broad range of liquids, exhibiting a water contact angle of 161.7 ± 2.2°, indicating non-wetting behavior. Notably, this approach enables rapid, large-area manufacturing, with a material removal rate of 1.068 mm3 s−1 over areas up to 1.5 × 104 mm2. The re-entrant textures retain sufficient structural features after 1000 abrasion cycles to recover superhydrophobicity. This geometry-guided strategy reveals a mechanism for the scalable fabrication of discrete microstructures and offers useful guidance for extending the approach to other machining modalities. Researchers fabricate re-entrant microstructures on metals through a confined shear-induced structure discretization (CSSD) mechanism using a cave-trapezoid cutting tool, resulting in durable, liquid-repellent surfaces.
